questions.prompt: The fractional miss of a feedback loop from its ideal feedback ratio is
questions.explanation: The closed loop reaches the ideal feedback ratio only as \(L\) grows. The fraction still missing is \(S = 1/(1+L)\). The complementary fraction \(L/(1+L)\) is the part that has arrived. \(1/L\) is the large-\(L\) approximation, not the exact miss.

questions.prompt: A loop has \(L = 24\). What is the fractional miss \(S = 1/(1+L)\)?
questions.explanation: \(S = 1/(1+24) = 1/25 = 0.04\). The approximation \(1/24\) is close and is not this value. The complementary fraction \(24/25\) is the part of the ideal ratio the loop does reach.

questions.prompt: Write the fractional miss \(S\) using the name \(L\) for the loop gain.
questions.explanation: The miss is \(1/(1+L)\). The form \(L/(1+L)\) is the complementary fraction, the part of the ideal ratio that is achieved. The form \(1/L\) drops the \(1\) in the denominator.

questions.prompt: A loop has \(L = 9\). What is the fractional miss \(1/(1+L)\)?
questions.explanation: \(1/(1+9) = 0.1\). The value \(1/9\) is the large-gain approximation. The value \(9/10\) is how much of the ideal ratio is achieved, not how much is missing.

questions.prompt: As \(|L|\) falls with frequency, the fractional miss
options: stays at its DC value, because \(S\) is defined at DC only
falls, because a smaller loop is a more accurate loop
questions.explanation: \(S = 1/(1+L)\) is larger when \(|L|\) is smaller. A loop that is accurate at low frequency becomes less accurate where the loop gain has rolled off. The miss is not equal to \(L\), and it is not frozen at the DC number.

questions.prompt: Order the steps from a loop gain to the fractional miss.
questions.explanation: The miss is the reciprocal of \(1+L\), so \(L\) comes first, then the sum, then the reciprocal. Reciprocal of \(L\) alone is the large-gain shortcut. Reciprocal of \(L/(1+L)\) is the complementary fraction turned upside down.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 330 186" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>loop gain falling as frequency rises</title><line x1="50" y1="156" x2="300" y2="156"/><polygon points="300,156 293.6,158.7 293.6,153.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="50" y1="156" x2="50" y2="30"/><polygon points="50,30 52.7,36.4 47.3,36.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="300" y="172" text-anchor="end" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">log ω</text><text x="54" y="26" text-anchor="start" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">|H| dB</text><polyline points="58,42 150,86 268,142" stroke-width="2.2"/><text x="96" y="52" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">−20</text><text x="188" y="96" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">−40</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A magnitude sketch that falls, then falls more steeply.
steps: Read the loop gain \(L\) at the frequency of interest.
Take the reciprocal of the sum.

questions.prompt: A note evaluates the miss of a loop with \(L = 4\). Exactly one step is wrong.
questions.explanation: \(1/(1+4) = 1/5\), while \(1/4\) is a different number. The shortcut \(1/L\) agrees with \(1/(1+L)\) only as \(L\) becomes large. The first, second, and last steps match the definition.

questions.prompt: At a high frequency, \(|L| = 3\). What is the fractional miss \(1/(1+|L|)\) used as the size of \(S\)?
questions.explanation: The size is \(1/(1+3) = 0.25\). A low-frequency loop gain would give a smaller miss. The value \(1/3\) drops the \(1\), and \(3/4\) is the complementary fraction.

questions.prompt: Which changes make the fractional miss \(1/(1+L)\) smaller?
options: Raising \(|L|\) at the frequency of interest
Keeping \(|L|\) large over a wider band
questions.explanation: The miss shrinks when \(|L|\) grows, including when that large gain extends to higher frequency. Substituting \(1/L\) is a different formula. Opening the loop sets \(L = 0\) and makes the miss \(1\).

questions.prompt: Preview of disturbance and tracking. A loop has \(L = 11\). The fraction \(S = 1/(1+L)\) is what a later skill multiplies onto an output disturbance. What is that fraction?
questions.explanation: \(S = 1/(1+11) = 1/12\). The disturbance reading uses this same fraction. The value \(11/12\) is the complementary fraction, and \(1/11\) is the large-gain shortcut.

questions.prompt: Preview of integral control. Why does a loop with infinite DC loop gain have no steady miss on a constant reference?
options: The junction stops subtracting at DC
A constant reference has no ideal feedback ratio
Infinite loop gain forces the phase to \(-180^\circ\)
questions.explanation: The steady miss on a constant reference is \(S(0) = 1/(1+L(0))\). An infinite DC loop gain drives that fraction to zero. A later skill gets that infinite DC gain from an integrator. The junction still subtracts, and the phase at DC is a different question.

questions.prompt: Preview of amplifier gain error. At the frequency of interest, \(|L| = 4\). What is the fractional miss \(1/(1+|L|)\)?
questions.explanation: The miss is \(1/(1+4) = 0.2\). An amplifier whose open-loop gain has fallen to this loop gain has the same fraction. The value \(0.25\) is \(1/|L|\), and \(0.8\) is the complementary fraction.
